event.detail:
Reviewed commit: 190d844e58c96cf197aa838d0b0eea8062f48435

TLDR: Considered whether an agent-requested environment could run a different launch after the user approves it, or claim the agent's choices as the user's defaults. The assigned change preserves the approved launch instead.

Details: AgentEnvironmentCreate (sessions.rs:1159-1169) stores TrustResolvedLaunch privately with serde(skip). for_agent_environment carries it and origin() chooses CreateOrigin::Agent. create_session_request:1848-1864 extracts that launch and passes it as FreshCreateContext.resolved_mode for a checkout, or uses it directly at 1877-1887 for a home-folder launch. create_fresh_session_resolved:2501-2506 uses the supplied mode without resolving trust again; its explicit_selection:2454-2464 is None for agent origin. The caller agent_requests.rs:4471-4493 resolves trust before the card and the same request is sent after approval at 4542. The browser cannot supply this private authority. Contract: SPEC_impl.md, Agent requests and environments, requires the card's direct Allow; SPEC.md, Agents and environments, says each environment launch always shows its own card with Allow and Deny only.

Suggested bucket: highest if an approved launch could silently change its security policy; that route is refuted here. Could-be-highest: yes, assessed explicitly. Confidence: confirmed by source, no execution. proposed_drop: source refutation above, not specification acceptance. possible_cover: none. Caveat: this is a review of the assigned sessions.rs change and its immediate caller, not a separate audit of every approval-card renderer.

No source premise was found for exchanging the environment binding in place underneath this connected refresh. TLDR: Investigated whether a sealed listing from an obsolete connection could authorize destroying a different current environment. The shipped retarget/adoption/resource-binding paths checked do not establish that route.

Adoption retires withdrawn clients and advances incarnation (2975-3000). Final destruction re-reads the row under its provisioning lock and targets its recorded binding.

Synthesis narrowed the binding premise: Podman store/podman.rs:415-433 admits a canonical container ID only if NULL or equal to the saved ID, so that provider enforces immutability in SQL. Tensorlake's set_tensorlake_sandbox_id (store.rs:7040-7064) does NOT enforce single-assignment in SQL; the earlier candidate must not be read as claiming it does. Its production callers supply the continuity: tensorlake/hosts.rs create_recorded:359-470 reads the current binding, checks its reserved name, looks up an existing resource by saved ID (by name only without one), and permits a fresh create only when sandbox_id is absent. Missing already-recorded IDs do not trigger replacement creation. delete_binding:550-600 uses a saved ID directly and recovers by name only for a pending create with no ID. The third caller found by git grep is cfg(test) plant. Podman ID enforcement and Tensorlake caller behavior therefore give the needed resource continuity without assuming a universal SQL invariant. Existing Tensorlake setup also refuses manager.is_sealed (provisioning/tensorlake_add.rs:890-898); setup and destruction share the host provisioning lock.

Suggested bucket: highest if unrelated current files/processes could be destroyed; that original consequence is preserved but no shipped route was established. Could-be-highest: yes. Confidence: confirmed source refutation of the considered transitions, no execution. proposed_drop: source refutation above, not specification acceptance of destructive stale targeting. possible_cover: none. Caveats: this relies on Tensorlake's lookup-by-ID returning that resource, as the existing provider contract already does. It does not claim the store setter itself is immutable, or cover external operator replacement/reset outside the checked transitions. Details: create_session_request captures SessionClaim and client in one host_client read at sessions.rs:1844-1846, uses that claim through either fresh-checkout creation (1852-1866) or ordinary creation (1894-1923), and returns the original pair. create_in_session_sandbox:1793-1794 then qualifies the SessionInfo ID with claim.entry_uuid and drops the rest of the claim. qualify_session_info:874-886 retains entry/session identity only; it carries no connection incarnation. Provisioning SessionLaunch.result at tensorlake_add.rs:101 and start_session_environment:353-355 transports only Result<SessionInfo>. finish_session_launch awaits completed-step publication and memory.lock at 1018-1026, then sends that session at 1057. No creating-connection claim survives to the receiver.

The provisioning guard is not a connection lease: setup explicitly release_hold at tensorlake_add.rs:613 before attach_supervisor; its remaining host_provision_lock excludes resource operations, not actor transport reconnection. manager run:3691-3745 executes connect_phase/serve and re-enters an active connection window after serve returns; serve independently notices client.closed at 4720. publish_refresh:5190-5207 assigns a new incarnation whenever the client changes, including withdrawal. Those paths therefore allow successful completion on connection A, then connection B before the separately scheduled receiver projects it, without retargeting the physical environment.

Contract: AgentSession.host (proto/lib.rs:2648-2658) pins every mutation reply, including creating replies, to the connection the mutation actually routed through. The ordinary projection contract at agent_requests.rs:4599-4631 requires the original routed claim for precisely this reason. # Later deletion and withdrawal changes leave canonical g024/l5 intact

## TLDR

Stopped environment actors can keep their manager, tasks and other host connections alive after the caller releases its last manager reference. One idle actor delays fallback cleanup until it leaves its wait; two persistently stopped actors with staggered waits can keep each other able to reacquire the manager indefinitely. This is the exact canonical g024/l5 event35 consequence, locally confirmed across the assigned later deletion changes, not an independent new discovery. Normal serving shutdown and the test restart path explicitly shut the manager down and remain protected.

## Details

Read complete own 19-event history and exact g024 events31-33/35 before revising. At original 566 manager.rs:3845-3893, let manager = self.manager.upgrade() creates a named Option<Arc<ConnectionManager>>. The gate borrows it; the only move into an owned start task is conditional on !stopped.attempted and gate. If either is false, that move is not evaluated and the initialized local survives the idle select loop inside the same arm. Independently consulted official Rust Reference local-variable drop scopes (https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/destructors.html#scopes-of-local-variables) and condition chains (https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/expressions/if-expr.html#chains-of-conditions): the named local belongs to its enclosing block; condition operands short-circuit left-to-right. Borrow last-use does not destroy this owned value early. The original manager self_ref docs :1161 expressly require Weak actor ownership so the manager/actor map can drop; ActorHandle :1075-1135 owns actor cancellation handles and connections.

Local interaction result: assigned 222 manager.rs:3298-3339 makes shutdown/shutdown_and_wait call withdraw_actors, which marks terminal shutdown, drains the actor map, withdraws clients and aborts actors. This cancels the idle future and drops the local Arc WHEN explicitly called. Drop :3342-3350 calls shutdown and cannot be reached while those strong references survive. Per-host hold_connection :1655-1695 retires that host's client and nudges it to park; release_hold :1702-1714 clears the hold and nudges again. stop_actor :3243-3259 removes and cancels only the selected actor. These operations can release that particular wait, but are not automatically invoked by losing the external manager owner. The new Deleting/seal maps and status/snapshot overlay do not end an idle Stopped arm or call global withdrawal. Their records contain phase/failure data, not a global lifetime cancellation signal.

The assigned host removal at hosts.rs:1506-1517 explicitly takes a Deleting hold for the selected host, later stopping its actor only on successful forgetting. Finisher :1450-1471 runs removal for already-sealed machine-deleting environments. An ordinary unsealed, gate-false Stopped episode requires no Delete, no seal and no connected listing. Therefore the fact that an actual Delete wakes a selected actor, or a sealed host projects Deleting, does not repair direct-drop fallback for the reachable ordinary stopped fleet. This interaction is separate from local l4 missing deletion-outcome writes and from g028/l3 stale captured finisher eligibility; no same-symptom merge or change to those findings is proposed.
